summary: In Greek mythology Pallas (Ancient Greek: Πάλλας) is, in Hesiod, the second-generation Titan son of Crius and Eurybia, brother of Astraeus and Perses, husband of the Oceanid Styx, and father of Zelus, Nike, Cratos, and Bia. He is sometimes styled a god of warcraft and the spring campaign season. The atlas keeps this Titan distinct from the Giant flayed by Athena (`pallas-giant`) and from the Athenian Pandionid (`pallas-pandionid`).
etymology: Ancient Greek Pállas (Πάλλας). The Suda links Athena's epithet "Pallas" to pallein, "to brandish" a spear — a separate aetiology from this Titan's name.

sections.heading: Hesiodic family
paragraphs: Hesiod's Theogony places Pallas among the children of Crius and Eurybia beside Astraeus and Perses. Joined to Styx he fathers Zelus (Emulation), Nike (Victory), Cratos (Strength), and Bia (Force) — the four who dwell forever beside Zeus after Styx comes first to his side in the Titan war. Hyginus, calling him "the giant," also gives Styx Scylla, Fontus ("Fountains"), and Lacus ("Lakes") by him — a Latin expansion kept separate from the Hesiodic core.

sections.heading: Other notes and homonyms
paragraphs: The Homeric Hymn to Hermes makes Selene daughter of a Pallas son of Megamedes — possibly the same figure. Ovid's patronymics Pallantias / Pallantis for Aurora treat Dawn as related to Pallas. Pausanias reports that Pellene in Achaea claimed naming from this Pallas, while Argives named it for an Argive Pellen.

Do not confuse this Titan with `pallas-giant` (flayed in the Gigantomachy for Athena's aegis), with `pallas-pandionid` (son of Pandion who revolts against Theseus), or with Athena's own cult title Pallas Athene.
